source.title: On the Limits of Sparse Autoencoders: A Theoretical Framework and Reweighted Remedy
source.authors: Jing-Yi Cui; Qi Zhang; Yi-Fei Wang; Yi-Sen Wang

record.tranche_reason: The paper derives and tests conditions under which SAEs recover or fail to recover ground-truth features, refining the scope of SAE-based feature recovery.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Toy Models of Superposition and adopts a superposition-based setup, but does not test whether ordinary networks develop the proposed overlapping, nearly orthogonal geometry or capacity allocation by feature importance. Reported SAE interpretability scores on language and vision models are proxy evaluations, not ground-truth feature-recovery measurements. Setup choices such as dimensions, layers, and selected weights are not separate results.
record.test_reason: The paper derives when SAE latents recover ground-truth sparse features in a superposition model. It shows that recovery generally fails (feature shrinking or vanishing) except under extreme sparsity, with synthetic validation. This bears directly on whether dictionary features are complete, canonical units (V5). The weighted-SAE experiments on real models only report the paper's own method against a baseline.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that standard SAEs suffer feature shrinking and vanishing and cannot fully recover ground-truth features except under extreme sparsity. They say full disentanglement is impossible under realistic sparsity, so SAE latents are approximate projections of overlapping features. They report that their reweighted SAE improves monosemanticity and interpretability proxies.
record.recipe_differences: The paper develops a theoretical SAE recovery framework and a reweighted loss; it is not a reproduction of the original toy-model method.
record.method_sensitivity: The theoretical recovery result depends on sparsity and interference assumptions. Empirical weighted-SAE scores vary by model layer and weighting parameter; the paper also reports a proxy sensitivity analysis.

fits_no_version.finding: WSAE lowers ground-truth reconstruction loss and raises per-dimension variance compared with a standard SAE at low sparsity, with comparable reconstruction of xp.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Variance-based reweighting of the SAE loss improves ground-truth recovery in synthetic superposition data without hurting input reconstruction.

fits_no_version.finding: Weighted SAE changes auto-interpretability scores on Pythia-160M and Llama-3-8B. Gains are mostly positive and depend on layer and α; two Pythia layers decrease slightly at α = 0.5.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weighted SAE objectives tend to increase LLM auto-interpretability scores, but effects vary by layer and weight.

fits_no_version.finding: Weighted SAE raises semantic consistency on ResNet-18 NCL embeddings: 40.2 → 40.7 (α = 0.5) and 42.2 (α = 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In vision embeddings, weighted SAE objectives increase semantic consistency of latents.

record.problems: The real-model experiments use proxy measures rather than ground-truth features. The synthetic plotted outcomes have no reported uncertainty in the supplied text. The theoretical and synthetic framework assumes a specified superposition mapping and does not establish that real networks use that representation. Table 3's listed gain for Llama-3-8B layer 16 does not equal the difference between its displayed SAE and WSAE scores.
record.rows_left_out: No results omitted for the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: The paper adopts a toy-model Wp (digon/polygon geometry, negative interference) as an assumption and as a data generator. It does not test whether networks learn that geometry or show the sparsity transition.
Capacity allocation by feature importance is not tested.
Incidental causes of polysemanticity are only cited (Lecomte et al.).
Real-model experiments report auto-interpretability and semantic-consistency scores of SAE latents. They do not test whether LLMs distribute features across neurons, and they have no ground truth.

Not tested: stability across seeds or dictionary sizes, whether SAE latents are canonical units in real LLMs (no ground truth there), and recovery under Top-k/JumpReLU beyond brief theoretical remarks.
Multi-dimensional features are not compared. The paper assumes scalar features throughout.

record.verdict_notes: The theoretical results are conditional on a linear superposition model xp = Wp x with digon/polygon (Theorem 1) or non-positive-interference (Theorems 2–3) geometry, taken from Toy Models. Recovery claims apply only within that model. The synthetic Wp is learned via the Toy Models ReLU output model; that is setup, not a V1 result. Table 2 (alternative Top-k) and Figure 5 (α/proxy sensitivity) are WSAE method results with no bearing on any version. ICLR 2026 paper; no uncertainty reported on synthetic figures.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test whether toy networks spontaneously store excess features as overlapping, nearly orthogonal directions, nor the regular geometry or sparsity-dependent transition in that storage.
No experiment tests capacity allocation according to feature importance or dedicated dimensions for important features.
The paper cites incidental causes of polysemanticity but does not test them.
The language-model experiments report SAE interpretability proxies, not whether LLM activations distribute features over neurons or whether SAEs recover ground-truth sparse features in LLMs.

Theoretical and synthetic tests address recovery completeness under the paper's assumptions. Stability across contexts, training runs, and alternative dictionaries, and whether SAE features are canonical units in real LLMs, are not tested.
The framework represents ground-truth features as scalar coordinates but does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: theoretical SAE framework
rows.operation_detail: Derives an optimal SAE solution and analyzes its ground-truth feature recovery
rows.measure: Ground-truth feature recovery from SAE latents
rows.value: The optimum is Wp transpose (up to row reordering and zero padding); recovered features can shrink or vanish and generally do not recover the ground truth.
rows.note: Analytical result; the theorem gives an optimum for reconstructing the polysemantic input, not a guarantee of ground-truth feature recovery.
rows.check: This is an analytic result, not an empirical one. Under general sparsity the optimum Wp^T yields shrunk or vanished features rather than the ground truth. Partial is an acceptable state.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.1, Theorem 1 and subsequent feature-recovery discussion

rows.measure: Ground-truth feature recovery and uniqueness of the optimum
rows.value: The optimum recovers the ground-truth features up to row reordering and zero padding; for nm = n the solution is unique.
rows.note: The recovery statement is conditional on the paper's extreme-sparsity and interference assumptions.

rows.operation_detail: Measures average number of ground-truth features activating each SAE latent

conditions.value: xi = 0 with probability S; xi sampled from U(0,1] otherwise

rows.measure: Average activated ground-truth features per SAE latent
rows.value: figure only; text reports a clear decrease as input sparsity increases
rows.note: This measures a proxy for SAE-latent monosemanticity across a sparsity sweep, not the network's feature-storage geometry.
rows.check: This is the paper's direct synthetic validation of SAE recovery versus sparsity, so it bears on V5 and should not be 'none'. The average number of ground-truth features per latent is roughly 2–4 in the figure and falls as sparsity rises, so latents are not monosemantic except at high sparsity. Values are figure-only.

relationships.condition: General (non-extreme) sparsity in the paper's linear superposition model and synthetic toy setup
relationships.reason: The closed-form optimum shrinks or zeroes polysemantic features. Example 1 gives (1.0, 0.8) → (0.2, 0) and Example 2 gives (0.7, 0.5, 0.3) → (0.3, 0, 0). In synthetic data, latents mix several ground-truth features at lower sparsity. Rows: th-general, example-shrink, example-vanish, synthetic-sparsity.
relationships.display_finding: The closed-form optimum shrank or zeroed polysemantic features, for example (1.0, 0.8) → (0.2, 0) and (0.7, 0.5, 0.3) → (0.3, 0, 0), and in synthetic data latents mixed several ground-truth features at lower sparsity.

relation.reason: The study derives recovery conditions and tests SAE latents against known synthetic ground-truth features.

tranche.reason: The theoretical results and synthetic validation directly contest complete SAE feature recovery under general sparsity.

source_check.notes: The theory uses a bias-free, tied-weight SAE with reconstruction-only loss; its recovery guarantees are conditional. Example 2's printed Wp is inconsistent with its subsequent Gram matrix, although equation 9 explicitly reports (0.3, 0, 0).

reader_labels.condition: General sparsity in the paper's theoretical framework and stated examples
reader_labels.reason: The optimal reconstruction of the polysemantic input need not recover ground-truth features, and examples show shrinking or vanishing; see th-general, example-shrink, and example-vanish.

reader_labels.reason: The theorem states full recovery, and uniqueness when nm = n, in this restricted setting; see th-extreme.
